metadata.summary: This ASPN guideline evaluates evidence for diagnosing and treating painful diabetic neuropathy and grades recommendations for available therapies. It covers pharmacological, topical, neuromodulation, other interventional, lifestyle, and psychological approaches, with an individualized treatment algorithm and considerations for implantable therapies in patients with diabetes. The recommendations are presented as best practices rather than a standard of care.

target_population: Patients with diabetes undergoing evaluation for painful diabetic neuropathy
Patients with painful diabetic neuropathy, including those with persistent pain despite conservative or pharmacological treatment
Patients with diabetes being considered for implantable therapies

conditions.name: painful diabetic neuropathy
conditions.description: A complication of diabetes mellitus involving persistent pain and altered sensation in the extremities. The guideline describes metabolic and vascular contributions to length-dependent nerve injury, including chronic hyperglycemia, oxidative stress and neuroinflammation.
conditions.epidemiology: PDN has been reported in as many as 16%–26% of people with diabetes. The guideline notes that it is often not discussed with patients and remains untreated.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms range from mild discomfort to disabling pain and may include tingling, electric-shock sensations, numbness, burning, or a sensation of walking on sandpaper or wearing extra socks. They often worsen at night. Sensory changes typically begin in the feet and toes, then extend proximally in a stocking-glove pattern. Sleep disturbance, anxiety and depression may accompany the pain.

subtypes.name: focal lower extremity PDN
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pain is relatively localized and may correspond predominantly to a single nerve territory, such as the plantar foot.

subtypes.name: diffuse PDN
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pain involves multiple nerve distributions and a sizeable dermatomal area.

subtypes.name: early-stage PDN
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Small nerve fibers may be affected before abnormalities become apparent on tests of large fibers; assessment of temperature sensation and intraepidermal nerve fibers may aid early detection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize symptoms and assess medical and family history, alcohol use, medications, underlying conditions and other possible causes of neuropathic pain.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation for suspected PDN, including early disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess sensory function, reflexes and motor strength.

diagnostic_workup.test: Toronto Diabetic Neuropathy Expert Group criteria
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide diagnostic criteria for diabetic neuropathy.
Assess vibration perception and large sensory nerve-fiber function.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Failure to perceive vibration indicates sensory impairment. An abnormal large-fiber test usually reflects a late, typically irreversible stage of disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess light-touch perception and large nerve-fiber function at sites that may include the plantar toes, metatarsal heads, dorsal hallux, midfoot and plantar heel.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The monofilament bends under 10 g of pressure. An abnormal large-fiber test usually reflects a late, typically irreversible stage of disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess temperature perception mediated by small nerve fibers.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced temperature perception may indicate early small-fiber involvement; standardization and subjectivity limit this test.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate perception of sharp stimuli and the function of small myelinated A-delta fibers.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Inability to identify a sharp stimulus indicates abnormal sensory function. The test is subjective but has high positive predictive value for PDN.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess reflex function, particularly at the Achilles tendon and patella.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Impaired reflexes warrant further investigation and are associated with abnormal nerve conduction velocity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess joint-position perception.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Studies cited by the guideline found a correlation between inaccurate proprioception and altered diabetic neuropathy scores.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure perception of sensory stimuli to evaluate small nerve-fiber function.
Contribute to initial screening for causes of peripheral neuropathy other than PDN.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Laboratory testing alone cannot establish PDN.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to initial assessment, including kidney function and possible alternative causes of neuropathy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Laboratory testing alone cannot establish PDN.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess blood glucose control.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Laboratory testing alone cannot establish PDN.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for another potential cause of peripheral neuropathy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Laboratory testing alone cannot establish PDN.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a possible vitamin-deficiency cause of neuropathy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Laboratory testing alone cannot establish PDN.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate monoclonal gammopathies associated with peripheral neuropathy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suggested by the AAN as part of laboratory evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess nerve damage and help exclude other possible causes of neuropathy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After a comprehensive history and examination, particularly when demyelination, nerve entrapment or nerve injury is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Their usefulness without suspicion of those conditions remains debatable; they do not provide the early small-fiber assessment available through skin biopsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assist treatment planning after clinical evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After a comprehensive history and examination, particularly when demyelination, nerve entrapment or nerve injury is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its usefulness without suspicion of those conditions remains debatable.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure intraepidermal nerve fiber densities for diagnosis and monitoring of early-stage PDN.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessment of early small-fiber involvement or disease progression is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The technique evaluates small fibers susceptible to early disease involvement and may indicate progression or treatment response.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess structural abnormalities or nerve compression.
Assess structural abnormalities or nerve compression.
Assess glycemic control, including before elective surgery involving an implantable therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Preoperatively in patients with diabetes undergoing elective surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline recommends delaying elective surgery for A1C above 8. It also states that there is no clear consensus on an A1C cutoff for elective surgery.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Small intraepidermal nerve fibers may show early disease involvement; the guideline describes reduced density in PDN.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Assessment by skin biopsy can support early diagnosis and monitoring of progression and may indicate treatment response.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline distinguishes early small-fiber involvement from the usually late, typically irreversible abnormalities detected by the described large-fiber sensory tests, but does not specify a formal staging system.

prognostic_tools.name: Michigan Diabetic Neuropathy Score (MDNS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: In the prospective SCS study cited by the guideline, a higher MDNS was associated with treatment failure during five years of follow-up (P = 0.014).

recommended_tests: Skin biopsy to assess intraepidermal nerve fiber densities when monitoring early disease progression or possible treatment response
long_term_effects: PDN can adversely affect physical and psychological quality of life.
Pain may be accompanied by sleep disturbance, anxiety and depression.

recognition: Peripheral edema may occur during gabapentin treatment.
prevention: Do not use gabapentin in patients with pre-existing peripheral edema.

toxicities.event: Reduced tolerance of TCA therapy and potential adverse effects
toxicities.incidence: One in five individuals cannot tolerate TCA therapy.
recognition: The guideline identifies narrow-angle glaucoma, benign prostatic hypertrophy, orthostasis, urinary retention, impaired liver function, and thyroid disease as conditions requiring particular caution.
Tricyclic anti-depressants may cause neurologic and cardiac adverse effects.
prevention: Use caution and monitor for adverse effects in patients with the specified conditions.

toxicities.event: QTc prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes
recognition: Assess the QTc interval in patients with additional cardiovascular risk factors.
prevention: Check the QTc interval in patients who have additional cardiovascular risk factors.

toxicities.event: Adverse consequences of long-term opioid use
recognition: The guideline identifies addiction and opioid-induced hyperalgesia with long-term opioid use.
The treatment algorithm identifies respiratory depression, sedation, opioid use disorder, and constipation as opioid-related safety concerns.
prevention: Opioids are generally not recommended for PDN because their safety profile is unfavorable despite modest short-term analgesia.
The guideline notes that several societies discourage tapentadol because of the adverse consequences of prolonged opioid use.

toxicities.event: Intolerance or adverse effects during oral analgesic treatment
recognition: The treatment algorithm identifies dizziness and sedation as adverse effects to monitor during oral analgesic treatment.
prevention: Increase the dose gradually toward an effective dose to reduce intolerance, and monitor for adverse effects.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Titrate gradually until an effective dose or the maximum allowable dose is reached. Gabapentin dosing requires adjustment in renal insufficiency.

toxicities.event: Drug-related adverse events during topical lidocaine or pregabalin treatment
toxicities.incidence: In the interim analysis by Baron et al, DRAE occurred in 3.9% of the lidocaine arm versus 39.2% of the pregabalin arm. Discontinuation due to DRAE was 13.% in the lidocaine arm versus 20.3% in the pregabalin arm.
The treatment algorithm states that application-site reactions with 8% topical capsaicin may affect over 30% of patients.
recognition: Skin irritation was reported as a reason for high dropout rates in studies of lower-dose capsaicin.
Capsaicin can initially produce warmth, itching, or pain.

Nausea, vomiting, confusion, postural hypotension, gait abnormality, urinary retention, nystagmus, drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, visual changes, and elevated serum creatine kinase are described; these effects are more common at higher doses.
prevention: The guideline recommends gradual upward titration because ziconotide has a narrow therapeutic window.
toxicities.dose_modifications: The recommended starting dose is 0.5–1.2 mcg/day per PACC, although product labeling permits a starting dose as high as 2.4 mcg/day. Recommended upward titration is 0.5–1.0 mcg/day every several days; the maximum dose is 21.6 μg/day.

toxicities.event: Psychiatric risk in patients with a history of psychosis
recognition: A history of psychosis is a contraindication identified in the ziconotide black box warning.
prevention: Complete a psychiatric evaluation before a ziconotide trial.
Do not use ziconotide in patients with a history of psychosis.

toxicities.event: Surgical-site infection and infection of an implanted device
toxicities.incidence: The guideline reports surgical-site infection rates of 1% to 17% across chronic-pain implantable devices. It cites an SCS infection rate as high as 3.11% within a 12-month period and an overall SCS implant infection rate of 2.45% in Hoelzer et al. In the 24-month report on 10kHz SCS, 3.2% of implants were explanted because of infection.
recognition: Diabetic patients, particularly those with poorly controlled DM, are described as having increased risk of infection and impaired wound healing.
Chronic hyperglycemia is associated with impaired neutrophil phagocytic activity and a relatively immunocompromised state.
prevention: Obtain preoperative A1c in diabetic patients undergoing elective surgery.
Delay elective surgery when A1C is above 8.
Attend to surgical technique to help limit postoperative infection.

toxicities.event: Poor wound healing, seroma, and wound dehiscence
recognition: Poorly controlled DM is described as increasing the risk of impaired healing and postoperative complications.
prevention: Attend to surgical technique to help limit seromas and wound dehiscence.
Obtain preoperative A1c in diabetic patients undergoing elective surgery and delay elective surgery when A1C is above 8.

toxicities.event: Harms associated with intensive glycemic control
recognition: The guideline associates tight glycemic control of hemoglobin A1C less than 6.0 with increased mortality.
The cited Ismail-Beigi et al study reports increased total and cardiovascular disease-related mortality, weight gain, and risk of severe hypoglycemia with intensive therapy.
In type 2 diabetes, intensive glycemic control may increase hypoglycemia risk without consistent benefit for preventing or treating PDN symptoms.
prevention: The guideline reports a recommendation for improved glycemic control with hemoglobin A1C between 7.0 and 8.0 instead of tight control below 6.0.

toxicities.event: Neuropathy associated with increased vitamin levels
recognition: The guideline states that increased levels can cause neuropathy.
toxicities.dose_modifications: No recommended dosing for safe treatment is available in the guideline.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Obtain preoperative A1c and postpone elective surgery when A1C is above 8.
Pay attention to surgical technique to help prevent postoperative infections, seromas, and wound dehiscence.
Perform a psychiatric evaluation before trialing ziconotide; a history of psychosis contraindicates its use.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Surgical-site infection associated with implantable therapies
infection_management.prevention: For diabetic patients undergoing elective surgery, obtain preoperative A1c and delay surgery when A1C is above 8. Attention to surgical technique may help reduce postoperative infection.

therapies_index.name: duloxetine
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, supporting descending pain-inhibitory pathways.
approved_indications: Approved for depression, anxiety, fibromyalgia, and generalized musculoskeletal pain
therapies_index.administration: Oral capsules of 20 mg, 30 mg, and 60 mg. The FDA target for PDN is 60 mg daily; doses in clinical practice range from 20 mg to 120 mg daily.

therapies_index.name: gabapentin
therapies_index.mechanism: Produces analgesia by binding to and inhibiting the α2δ-1 receptor of a voltage-gated calcium channel.
approved_indications: FDA-approved for seizures and post-herpetic neuralgia
therapies_index.administration: Used for PDN without FDA approval for that indication. Oral capsules of 100 mg, 300 mg, and 400 mg; tablets of 600 mg and 800 mg; and liquid at 250 mg/5 mL. Clinical PDN regimens range from 300 mg three times daily to 1200 mg three times daily, with a maximum of 3600 mg/day. Adjust the dose in renal insufficiency.
key_toxicities: Peripheral edema
monitoring: Assess renal function when selecting the dose.
Assess for pre-existing peripheral edema; the guide advises against use in those patients.

therapies_index.name: pregabalin
therapies_index.mechanism: Acts through a mechanism described as similar to that of gabapentin.
approved_indications: FDA-approved for neuropathic pain from PDN, post-herpetic neuralgia, and spinal cord injury
Used for fibromyalgia and partial onset seizure
therapies_index.administration: Oral capsules of 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg, 225 mg, and 300 mg, or liquid at 20 mg/mL. For PDN, the FDA recommends a maximum of 300 mg per day divided into 3 doses; the guide also describes a clinical maximum of 300 mg per day.
key_toxicities: Drug-related adverse events occurred in the pregabalin comparison arm of a topical lidocaine study.

therapies_index.name: amitriptyline
therapies_index.mechanism: As a TCA, is described as inhibiting norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake and blocking sodium channels. The guide also describes NMDA receptor antagonism and calcium-channel blockade; the precise mechanism of its topical formulation remains uncertain.
therapies_index.administration: Studied orally at 25 to 75 mg per day in one comparison; another study identified 150 mg per day as an optimal daily dose among patients able to tolerate higher concentrations. Topical formulations studied include 5% amitriptyline and 2% amitriptyline.
key_toxicities: TCA treatment may be intolerable for one in five individuals.
The guide cautions about adverse effects in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma, benign prostatic hypertrophy, orthostasis, urinary retention, impaired liver function, or thyroid disease.
QTc prolongation may pose a risk of torsades de pointes.
monitoring: Monitor for adverse effects associated with TCA treatment.
Assess the QTc interval in patients with additional cardiovascular risk factors.

therapies_index.name: nortriptyline
key_toxicities: The guide notes that tricyclic antidepressants used as oral analgesics commonly have neurologic and cardiac adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: tapentadol
therapies_index.mechanism: Acts centrally through opioid receptor agonism and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited trials, treatment was titrated during a three-week open-label period before randomized maintenance treatment.
key_toxicities: The guide cites addiction risk with long-term opioid use.
As an opioid analgesic, it carries a risk of opioid-related adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine
therapies_index.mechanism: Reversibly blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in neuronal membranes, reducing nerve impulse transmission.
therapies_index.administration: Applied topically; studies evaluated a 5% lidocaine patch or plaster.

therapies_index.name: capsaicin
therapies_index.mechanism: Activates TRPV1 on sensory fibers. Sustained high-concentration exposure desensitizes and reversibly defunctionalizes nociceptive fibers, reducing pain signaling.
approved_indications: The 8% capsaicin patch is FDA-approved for PDN; the algorithm specifies PDN of the feet.
therapies_index.administration: Topical preparations discussed include 0.075% capsaicin cream, an 8% capsaicin patch, and 0.75% ointment in the recommendations table. The guide reports that a single application of the 8% patch can relieve focal neuropathic pain for up to 12 weeks.
key_toxicities: Warmth, itching, or pain may occur with initial TRPV1 activation.
Skin irritation contributed to discontinuation in studies of lower-concentration preparations.
Application-site reactions with the 8% patch may affect over 30% of patients.

therapies_index.name: ziconotide
therapies_index.mechanism: Binds N-type voltage-sensitive calcium channels and reversibly inhibits release of pronociceptive neurotransmitters from afferent nerves in the spinal cord dorsal horn.
approved_indications: FDA-approved for administration through a microambulatory delivery device
therapies_index.administration: Intrathecal administration only. The PACC starting dose is 0.5–1.2 mcg/day; product labeling permits a starting dose as high as 2.4 mcg/day. The guide recommends increasing by 0.5–1.0 mcg/day every several days, up to 21.6 μg/day.
key_toxicities: Nausea
Vomiting
Confusion
Postural hypotension
Gait abnormality
Urinary retention
Nystagmus
Drowsiness
Dizziness
Weakness
Visual changes
Serum creatine kinase elevation
The drug carries a black box warning and is contraindicated in patients with a history of psychosis.
monitoring: Complete a psychiatric evaluation before a medication trial.
Titrate cautiously because of the narrow therapeutic window.

therapies_index.name: morphine
approved_indications: FDA-approved for chronic intractable pain when used for intrathecal drug delivery
therapies_index.administration: The guide mentions intrathecal morphine use but provides no PDN dosing regimen.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin type A
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions and may modulate sensory fiber activity by inhibiting glutamate release and decreasing release of calcitonin gene related peptide and substance P.
therapies_index.administration: Studied as an intradermal injection into the foot for PDN; injection for PDN is not an FDA-approved indication.

therapies_index.name: Alpha-lipoic acid
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as an antioxidant and chemoprotective compound.
therapies_index.administration: One cited study used oral 600mg once daily for 5 weeks; the guide does not establish a recommended dose for safe PDN treatment.

therapies_index.name: vitamin B complex (B1, B6, B12)
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide describes antioxidant effects and roles in neural metabolism and protection.
therapies_index.administration: No recommended dose for safe PDN treatment is established in the guide.
key_toxicities: Increased levels can cause neuropathy.

therapies_index.name: Saussureae Involucratae Herba
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide describes proposed effects on blood circulation and oxidative processes.
therapies_index.administration: Studied as injections at acupuncture points.

therapies_index.name: duloxetine (60 mg/day) and pregabalin (300 mg/day)
therapies_index.administration: A cited study evaluated duloxetine 60 mg/day combined with pregabalin 300 mg/day.

therapies_index.name: spinal cord stimulation
therapies_index.mechanism: Neuromodulation acts on ascending pathways involved in pain perception.
therapies_index.administration: For PDN, the guide describes a temporary trial of approximately 7 days before deciding on permanent surgical implantation.
key_toxicities: Implant infection is a concern in patients with diabetes.
monitoring: Obtain preoperative A1c in diabetic patients undergoing elective surgery.
The guide recommends delaying elective surgery for A1C above 8.

therapies_index.name: traditional SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides spinal cord stimulation using a perceptible, low-frequency stimulation cycle.
therapies_index.administration: Studied with conventional medical therapy for lower-extremity PDN unresponsive to medical treatment.
key_toxicities: Implant infection is a concern in patients with diabetes.
monitoring: Assess response during trial stimulation before permanent implantation.

therapies_index.name: burst SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Delivers subthreshold spinal cord stimulation in bursts; the guide describes its pattern as designed to resemble thalamic Theta burst activity.
therapies_index.administration: A cited crossover study used burst SCS for two weeks after six months of traditional SCS.

therapies_index.name: 10-kHz SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides subthreshold spinal cord stimulation that is not consciously perceived.
therapies_index.administration: Studied for PDN alongside conventional medical management.
key_toxicities: Infection led to explantation of 3.2% of implants in the cited 24-month report.

therapies_index.name: PNS
therapies_index.mechanism: Stimulates a selected peripheral nerve to address pain within its distribution.
therapies_index.administration: Temporary and permanent systems are described. Potential targets include the tibial, common peroneal, superficial peroneal, sciatic, median, and ulnar nerves; the guide advises considering lead placement proximal to a suspected lesion, entrapment, or injury.
key_toxicities: Stimulating motor fibers rather than selectively targeting sensory fibers is a procedural concern.

therapies_index.name: DRG-S
therapies_index.mechanism: Modulates sensory signaling at the dorsal root ganglion; the guide also describes possible effects on neuronal hypersensitivity and inflammatory responses.
approved_indications: Approved for CRPS and/or peripheral causalgia in the groin and lower limb
therapies_index.administration: Investigated for lower-extremity PDN; one cited series used trial leads at L4-S1.

therapies_index.name: mPNS
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses a changing magnetic field to induce electrical stimulation of peripheral nerve tissue; the guide describes recruitment of Aβ fibers without recruitment of Aδ fibers at the stimulation threshold.
therapies_index.administration: In a cited pilot, an active treatment wand was placed on or just above the skin. Treatment comprised three consecutive daily sessions in the first week, followed by weekly sessions for the rest of the month, totaling 6 treatments; sessions occurred every second week in the second month, with monthly treatment as needed for pain exacerbations.

therapies_index.name: ePNS
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses an electrical field to stimulate peripheral nerves; the guide contrasts its field with that induced by mPNS.
key_toxicities: Higher current density near the skin surface can cause tissue damage.

therapies_index.name: PENS
therapies_index.administration: A cited study applied percutaneous electrical stimulation to lower-extremity nerves, including the tibial and deep peroneal nerves.

therapies_index.name: intrathecal drug delivery
therapies_index.administration: Delivers medication by the intrathecal route. The guide discusses careful selection for ziconotide therapy in diabetic neuropathic pain while noting the absence of studies specifically testing its effectiveness for PDN.

therapies_index.name: nerve blocks
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned as an interventional option for refractory PDN.

therapies_index.name: lumbar sympathetic block
therapies_index.administration: Discussed for selected patients with refractory PDN. Cited approaches include continuous blocks and combination with alcohol neurolysis.

therapies_index.name: alcohol neurolysis
therapies_index.administration: Studied for PDN alone and after continuous lumbar sympathetic block; a cited comparison also evaluated combination with radiofrequency thermocoagulation.

therapies_index.name: radiofrequency thermocoagulation
therapies_index.administration: Studied for PDN alone and in combination with alcohol neurolysis.

therapies_index.name: decompression neurolysis
therapies_index.administration: Described for nerves of the upper and lower extremities in patients with diabetes.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin injection
therapies_index.administration: Studies cited in the guide used intradermal botulinum toxin type A injection into the foot. Injection for PDN is not an FDA-approved indication.

therapies_index.name: perineural platelet rich plasma
therapies_index.administration: A cited study used ultrasound-guided perineural platelet rich plasma injection alongside medical treatment.

therapies_index.name: acupuncture
therapies_index.administration: If used for PDN, the guide recommends the semi-standardized ACUDPN protocol with bilateral acupuncture points.

therapies_index.name: electroacupuncture
therapies_index.mechanism: Applies electrical current to acupuncture needles.
therapies_index.administration: Electrical current is delivered through acupuncture needles.

therapies_index.name: physical therapy
therapies_index.administration: The algorithm advises offering it early in PDN; examples include long-term aerobic exercise, weight-bearing exercise, and massage therapy.

therapies_index.name: aerobic exercise
therapies_index.administration: Described as a long-term component of early physical therapy for PDN.

therapies_index.name: weight-bearing exercise
therapies_index.administration: Described as a component of early physical therapy for PDN.

therapies_index.name: massage therapy
therapies_index.administration: Described as a component of early physical therapy for PDN.

therapies_index.name: glycemic control
therapies_index.mechanism: Addresses hyperglycemia, which the guide identifies as a possible contributor to nerve dysfunction and painful neural pathways.
therapies_index.administration: Presented as an initial management strategy. The guide distinguishes the evidence and risks of intensive control in T1DM from those in T2DM.
key_toxicities: The guide associates tight glycemic control with increased mortality and notes a risk of hypoglycemia with intensive control in type 2 diabetes.

therapies_index.name: weight loss
therapies_index.administration: Discussed as a lifestyle measure for PDN.

therapies_index.name: CBT
therapies_index.administration: Studied as a psychological treatment for PDN, including delivery alongside standard pharmacological care.

therapies_index.name: MT
therapies_index.administration: Discussed as a psychological approach encompassing MM or MBSR.

therapies_index.name: MM
therapies_index.administration: Studied for PDN as mindfulness meditation training, including a cited study using 16 sessions with unspecified elements of cognitive therapy.

therapies_index.name: MBSR
therapies_index.administration: Studied as a psychological treatment for PDN.

therapies_index.name: ACT
therapies_index.administration: A cited PDN trial provided 8 sessions.

therapies_index.name: relaxation training
therapies_index.administration: Studied as a psychological intervention for PDN.

therapies_index.name: progressive relaxation meditation
therapies_index.administration: A cited study provided 16 sessions.

special_populations.population: Diabetic patients undergoing elective surgery for implantable therapies
special_populations.considerations: Diabetes increases the risk of impaired wound healing and surgical site infection. A1C can help identify poor glycemic control, although the document notes no agreed A1C threshold for elective surgery. Cited studies associate A1C >8% with poorer surgical outcomes and increased postoperative surgical site infections.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Obtain preoperative A1c and delay elective surgery when A1C is above 8.

special_populations.considerations: Gabapentin is eliminated primarily through the kidneys.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Adjust the gabapentin dose in patients with renal insufficiency.
Do not use gabapentin in patients who already have peripheral edema.

special_populations.population: Patients with concomitant depression, anxiety, fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, or mood disorder
special_populations.considerations: Coexisting conditions can inform analgesic selection. Duloxetine also has indications for depression, anxiety, fibromyalgia, and generalized musculoskeletal pain; amitriptyline treats depression.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Duloxetine can be an appropriate choice when the listed conditions coexist with PDN. Consider amitriptyline when a mood disorder accompanies PDN.

special_populations.population: Patients with conditions that increase concern about TCA adverse effects
special_populations.considerations: The document identifies narrow-angle glaucoma, benign prostatic hypertrophy, orthostasis, urinary retention, impaired liver function, and thyroid disease as reasons for particular caution. Additional cardiovascular risk factors warrant assessment of the QTc interval because of the risk of torsades de pointes.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Monitor for adverse effects when considering TCAs. Assess QTc in patients with additional cardiovascular risk factors, and consider an alternative if the interval is prolonged.

special_populations.population: Patients with a history of psychosis
special_populations.considerations: Ziconotide has a black box warning and is contraindicated in this population.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use ziconotide; complete a psychiatric evaluation before a trial of the medication.

special_populations.population: Patients with type 1 DM or type 2 DM
special_populations.considerations: Intensive glycemic control may delay the development or progression of PDN in type 1 DM. It has shown little consistent benefit for PDN in type 2 DM and may increase the risk of hypoglycemia; tight control in type 2 DM may also increase mortality.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Individualize glycemic management by diabetes type. The document recommends improved glycemic control with hemoglobin A1C between 7.0 and 8.0 rather than tight control with hemoglobin A1C less than 6.0.

special_populations.population: Patients with focal lower extremity PDN who are not candidates for SCS
special_populations.considerations: PNS may suit pain localized to a single nerve distribution. It may be useful when complex spine anatomy, prior spinal surgery or fusion, or inability to discontinue anticoagulants makes SCS unsuitable. Diffuse pain spanning multiple nerve distributions may not be adequately covered by current PNS systems.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider PNS after conservative therapies have failed if the patient is not a candidate for SCS. When planning lead placement, consider a position proximal to a suspected lesion, entrapment, or injury.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with diabetes, including those with established PDN.
decision_rules: Assess patients with diabetes for PDN and its effects on function and quality of life.
Individualize treatment according to comorbidities, diabetes type and severity, and patient preferences.
Address hyperglycemia and offer conservative measures early; oral analgesics may be started afterward or alongside them.

recommended_regimens.name: physical therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer early in PDN; long-term aerobic exercise, weight-bearing exercise, and massage therapy may improve neuropathy-related motor and sensory problems, balance, and quality of life.

supportive_care: Discuss achievable goals for pain reduction and functional improvement; complete elimination of pain is not a realistic expectation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Management is multimodal and may involve primary care, endocrinology, interventional pain medicine, podiatry, and other disciplines.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with Type 1 DM.
decision_rules: Use improved glycemic control as part of prevention and early management; intensive control may delay PDN development or progression in this population.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle modification
recommended_regimens.summary: Improve glycemic control and combine dietary improvement with an active lifestyle to help limit PDN symptoms.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The DCCT reported a −1.84 annualized risk difference with tight glycemic control in T1DM.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence for intensive glycemic control is more favorable in type 1 diabetes than in type 2 diabetes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with Type 2 DM.
decision_rules: Improve glycemic control as part of diabetes care, without assuming that intensive control will prevent or relieve PDN.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle modification
recommended_regimens.summary: Use improved glycemic control, diet, and activity while accounting for the limited effect of intensive control on PDN in Type 2 DM.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The ACCORD and VADT studies reported an annualized risk difference of −0.058 for T2DM, which was not statistically significant.

not_recommended.name: tight glycemic control of hemoglobin A1C less than 6.0
not_recommended.reason: The guideline associates this level of control with increased mortality and describes an increased risk of hypoglycemia with intensive control in type 2 diabetes.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes hemoglobin A1C between 7.0 and 8.0 as a recommended range for improved glycemic control.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients requiring oral pain treatment; selection should account for depression, anxiety, seizure disorder, peripheral edema, and renal failure.
decision_rules: Offer medications from the SNRI, gabapentinoids, and TCAs classes.
Select an agent according to comorbidities and adverse-effect profiles.
Increase the dose gradually until benefit or the maximum allowable dose is reached; do not judge an inadequately dosed or insufficiently tested agent ineffective.

recommended_regimens.name: duloxetine
recommended_regimens.summary: An FDA-approved oral option for PDN that may be particularly suitable when depression, anxiety, fibromyalgia, or musculoskeletal pain coexists. The FDA target dose is 60 mg daily; clinical practice doses range from 20 mg to 120 mg daily.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a placebo-controlled study, 24-hour average pain improved significantly after 12 weeks with 60 mg daily or 60 mg twice daily compared with 20 mg daily or placebo. In another study, duloxetine 60 mg daily performed significantly better than pregabalin 300 mg daily across BPI domains after 8 weeks.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: An agent may be considered ineffective if it has not worked after 12 weeks at the maximum allowable dose.

recommended_regimens.name: pregabalin
recommended_regimens.summary: An FDA-approved option for neuropathic pain from PDN. The FDA recommends no more than 300 mg per day divided into 3 doses.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a randomized trial, pregabalin 300 mg per day (100 mg three times daily) significantly improved pain VAS scores versus placebo after 8 weeks.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: An agent may be considered ineffective if it has not worked after 12 weeks at the maximum allowable dose.

recommended_regimens.name: gabapentin
recommended_regimens.summary: An oral option used for PDN without FDA approval for this indication. Clinical practice doses range from 300 mg three times daily to 1200 mg three times daily; the maximum is 3600 mg/day.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A randomized trial found greater symptom reduction than placebo on a VAS after 8 weeks of treatment.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: An agent may be considered ineffective if it has not worked after 12 weeks at the maximum allowable dose.

alternative_regimens.name: amitriptyline
alternative_regimens.summary: A TCA option for neuropathic pain that may be considered instead of other recommended treatments, particularly when a mood disorder coexists.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider tolerability, anticholinergic and cardiovascular risks, and relevant comorbidities.

alternative_regimens.name: desipramine
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited randomized study found pain relief comparable to amitriptyline.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The cited study presented it as an alternative for patients unable to tolerate amitriptyline.

not_recommended.name: opioids
not_recommended.reason: Despite modest to moderate PDN pain relief, their use is not recommended because of adverse effects and the unfavorable safety profile of longer-term treatment.

response_assessment.method: Assess therapeutic benefit after escalation to the maximum allowable dose, if tolerated.
response_assessment.interpretation: The medication may be considered ineffective if adequate efficacy has not been achieved after this dose and duration.

supportive_care: Discuss pain-control and functional goals before treatment.
Monitor for adverse effects during titration, including dizziness and sedation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Gabapentin requires dose adjustment in renal insufficiency and should not be used with pre-existing peripheral edema. The guideline's Grade A, Level I recommendation applies to offering the SNRI, gabapentinoids, and TCAs classes; it does not assign separate grades to individual drugs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considering oral agents from different medication classes together.
decision_rules: Weigh the potential advantages and disadvantages individually; the evidence is inadequate to recommend either for or against combination treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: duloxetine and pregabalin
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited study compared duloxetine (60 mg/day) plus pregabalin (300 mg/day) with high-dose duloxetine (120 mg/day) and pregabalin (600 mg/day); combination treatment was not more effective than individual-agent treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider only after an individualized assessment of benefits and disadvantages; evidence for combinations is limited.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation on combination therapy is graded C, Level II, with Low certainty of net benefit.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose conservative and FDA-approved treatments have failed, or whose drug-related adverse events prevent titration of oral medication.
decision_rules: Consider topical treatment when oral analgesia is insufficient or adverse effects restrict its use.

recommended_regimens.name: topical lidocaine
recommended_regimens.summary: May be offered as an adjunct to an individualized PDN treatment plan after conservative and FDA-approved options fail or oral-agent titration is limited by DRAE.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In Baron et al's interim analysis, the lidocaine and pregabalin arms had DRAE rates of 3.9% and 39.2%, respectively. The full analysis reported significantly greater EQ-5D quality-of-life improvement with lidocaine.

recommended_regimens.name: topical capsaicin 0.75% ointment
recommended_regimens.summary: May be offered as a 2nd line option after conservative and FDA-approved treatments fail or DRAE limit oral dose titration.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The topical recommendation specifies 0.75% ointment, while the discussion of earlier capsaicin cream trials specifies 0.075%; the document does not reconcile these concentrations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with PDN, particularly when initial oral agents are ineffective or yield only partial relief; the treatment algorithm specifies PDN of the feet after failure of at least two proven oral pharmacological agents.
decision_rules: Consider the FDA-approved patch alongside FDA-approved oral medication.
Account for application-site reactions when deciding whether the patch is tolerable.

recommended_regimens.name: 8% capsaicin patch
recommended_regimens.summary: May provide moderate benefit for PDN in conjunction with FDA-approved oral medication; the treatment algorithm also presents it as an option after at least two proven oral agents fail.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In Simpson et al, mean change in average daily pain from baseline to weeks 2–8 was −27.4% with capsaicin and −20.9% with placebo (p<0.001). In Anand et al, the capsaicin group had an NRS change of −1.87 at 12 week follow up (p=0.0001), versus −.58 in the comparison group (p=0.11).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: A cited review reported relief for up to 12 weeks after a single application.

response_assessment.interpretation: This was the assessment period in the cited Simpson et al trial.
This was the follow-up assessment in the cited Anand et al trial.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The treatment algorithm states that application-site reactions may affect over 30% of patients.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose first- and second-line therapeutic agents have failed.
decision_rules: Do not use topical amitriptyline as first-line PDN treatment; consider later use only with recognition of conflicting efficacy evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: topical amitriptyline
alternative_regimens.summary: May yield marginal pain improvement and may have fewer DRAE than some comparators; the recommendation is Grade C.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider for PDN refractory to first- and second-line agents rather than as first-line treatment.

not_recommended.name: topical amitriptyline as first-line treatment
not_recommended.reason: The literature on its efficacy is conflicting.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In Ho et al's mixed-neuropathic-pain trial, topical 5% amitriptyline did not produce a clinically meaningful advantage over placebo; the PDN subgroup was small. Kiani et al found topical 2% amitriptyline and 0.75% capsaicin cream both effective, with fewer DRAE and better adherence in the amitriptyline arm.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom other oral analgesics are being considered.
decision_rules: Recognize that tapentadol is FDA-approved for PDN but that its opioid-related risks affect treatment selection.

alternative_regimens.name: tapentadol
alternative_regimens.summary: An FDA-approved PDN analgesic that showed benefit in cited randomized trials after open-label titration, but is an opioid with risks associated with longer-term use.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The algorithm lists it among other oral analgesics that may be trialed when initial agents do not provide meaningful relief or cause intolerable effects.

not_recommended.name: tapentadol
not_recommended.reason: Despite its FDA indication, the guideline reports that several societies discourage it and that the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology clinical Practice Guideline recommends against opioids, including tapentadol, for PDN because of addiction risk with long-term opioid use.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Its FDA approval and the cited external recommendation against its use are distinct positions presented by the guideline.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with lower extremity PDN after failure of other non-invasive FDA-approved treatments.
decision_rules: Consider SCS when conventional medical management has not achieved benefit.
A temporary stimulation trial of approximately 7 days can assess benefit before permanent implantation.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: The committee recommends considering SCS for eligible lower-extremity PDN. Both traditional SCS and HF-SCS have shown better pain relief than conventional medical management in randomized trials.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In De Vos et al, mean VAS changed from 73 at baseline to 31 after six months with traditional SCS (P<0.001), versus 67 at both timepoints in controls (P = 0.97). In SENZA-PDN, 78.9% (75/95) of the HF-SCS arm and 5.3% (5/94) of the CMM arm achieved >50% pain relief without neurological deterioration at six months (P < 0.001).

recommended_regimens.name: 10 kHz high frequency (HF)-SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: A studied SCS approach for PDN that has not responded adequately to medical management.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In follow-up of the SENZA-PDN trial, investigators reported mean pain relief of 74.3% and >50% pain relief without further neurological decline in 85% of implanted patients at 12 months. At 24 months, mean pain reduction from baseline was 79.9%, and 90.1% of participants had greater than 50% relief.

alternative_regimens.name: burst SCS
alternative_regimens.summary: In the cited crossover study, burst stimulation relieved pain more than traditional SCS in a PDN subset, but PDN-specific investigation remains limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The studied patients had previously received traditional SCS for six months before a two-week burst SCS period.

response_assessment.method: Temporary SCS trial before permanent implantation
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the trial to gauge efficacy.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For implanted diabetic patients, obtain preoperative A1c for elective surgery and delay elective surgery when A1C is above 8, as recommended elsewhere in the guideline. A higher MDNS was associated with treatment failure over five years in Van Beek et al (P = 0.014).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with focal lower extremity PDN who have failed conservative therapies and are not candidates for SCS.
decision_rules: Consider PNS when pain is localized sufficiently to target a peripheral nerve.
Diffuse pain across multiple nerve distributions may not be adequately covered by available PNS leads.
Consider placing a lead proximal to a suspected lesion, entrapment, or injury.

recommended_regimens.name: PNS
recommended_regimens.summary: The committee recommends consideration for focal lower-extremity PDN after conservative treatment failure when SCS is unsuitable.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A plantar-foot pain focus may be addressed through tibial nerve targeting; other described lower-extremity targets include the common peroneal, superficial peroneal, and sciatic nerves. PNS may be useful when spinal anatomy, prior surgery or fusion, or inability to discontinue anticoagulants makes SCS or DRG-S unsuitable. The PDN-specific evidence remains limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with lower extremity PDN who have failed other FDA-approved treatments.
decision_rules: Consider DRG-S selectively and judiciously, taking professional judgment and previous treatment failures into account.

alternative_regimens.name: DRG-S
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered for lower-extremity PDN after other FDA-approved treatments fail; the recommendation is Grade C, and PDN-specific evidence is limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Reserve selection for an individualized assessment of prior treatments and likely focal coverage.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline identifies retrospective designs, lack of blinding, and small patient numbers as evidence limitations. In Eldabe et al, three of seven fully implanted patients achieved ≥50% pain reduction at six months; two achieved ≥50% at 12 months, with one patient lost to follow-up.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Carefully selected patients with diabetic neuropathic pain being considered for intrathecal treatment.
decision_rules: Consider the limited, indirect evidence for PDN before selecting intrathecal therapy.
Complete psychiatric evaluation before a ziconotide trial and do not use it in patients with a history of psychosis.

alternative_regimens.name: intrathecal ziconotide
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline supports careful selection for intrathecal treatment but rates evidence supporting ziconotide for diabetic neuropathy as limited; the recommendation is Grade C.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider only after individualized assessment, including the psychiatric contraindication. Published studies specifically investigating effectiveness for PDN are absent.

not_recommended.name: ziconotide in patients with a history of psychosis
not_recommended.reason: The medication is contraindicated in this population and carries a black box warning.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: PACC recommends starting at 0.5–1.2 mcg/day and increasing by 0.5–1.0 mcg/day every several days; product labeling permits a starting dose as high as 2.4 mcg/day, and the maximum is 21.6 μg/day. Trials cited for intrathecal ziconotide address non-cancer-related pain rather than PDN specifically.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with PDN considering non-invasive neuromodulation.
decision_rules: mPNS may be considered as a non-invasive treatment, while recognizing that PDN-specific evidence remains limited.

recommended_regimens.name: mPNS
recommended_regimens.summary: May provide intermediate-term relief of neuropathic pain due to PDN.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a reported study, 8 out of 8 PDN patients assessed per protocol in the active-treatment arm were responders at 3 months, with pain scores reduced by 64.7%; 1 out of 4 in the control arm responded, with average pain scores increasing by 2.4%.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 3 months of intermediate-term benefit are specified in the recommendation.

response_assessment.interpretation: The cited study defined response as >50% pain relief after treatment initiation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes ongoing research and does not establish mPNS as a proven frontline PDN treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considering a non-implantable adjunctive treatment.
decision_rules: Acupuncture may be considered as an optional PDN treatment.
If it is tried, use the semi-standardized ACUDPN protocol with bilateral acupuncture points.

recommended_regimens.name: Acupuncture
recommended_regimens.summary: May be considered; cited studies suggest possible benefit with relatively low adverse-event rates.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In Chao et al, average weekly pain improved versus usual care at week 12 but returned to baseline by week 18.

alternative_regimens.name: Electroacupuncture
alternative_regimens.summary: Cited research reported reductions in neuropathic pain alongside improvements in sleep and quality of life.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Presented as a studied modification of acupuncture, without a separate formal recommendation.

alternative_regimens.name: Laser acupuncture
alternative_regimens.summary: Cited research reported improved nerve conduction velocities and patient-reported outcomes versus placebo.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Presented as a studied modification of acupuncture, without a separate formal recommendation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline calls for further study of the durability of benefit.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients with refractory PDN being considered individually before more invasive interventions.
decision_rules: Consider lumbar sympathetic interventions case by case; additional safety and long-term outcome evidence is needed.

alternative_regimens.name: Lumbar Sympathetic Block and Neurolysis
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered on a case-by-case basis; the recommendation is Grade C.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected refractory PDN when the limited evidence and unresolved longer-term safety questions are acceptable.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited comparison reported complete remission rates of 66.7%, 73.3% and 93.3% after alcohol neurolysis, radiofrequency thermocoagulation, and combined treatment, respectively; pain returned at 3 months, 6 months and 1 year, respectively.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with PDN receiving first-line treatment who are being considered for an adjunct.
decision_rules: Consider botulinum toxin injection only as an adjunct to first-line modalities because the observed analgesic effect is small.

alternative_regimens.name: Botulinum Toxin Injection
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered as adjunctive PDN treatment; studies suggest pain and quality-of-life benefits, but the effect size is small. The recommendation is Grade C.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use alongside, rather than instead of, first-line approaches.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Botulinum toxin injection for PDN is not an FDA-approved indication, and the guideline calls for further research.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considering dietary supplementation for PDN symptoms.
decision_rules: Do not make a recommendation either for or against supplements on the available comparative evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: Alpha Lipoic Acid
alternative_regimens.summary: Studies cited by the guideline report symptom improvement, but comparative efficacy against usual PDN medications has not been established.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The Grade C supplements statement is neither favorable nor unfavorable and provides no recommended safe dose.

alternative_regimens.name: Acetyl-L-Carnitine
alternative_regimens.summary: Cited studies report benefit, but high-grade comparative evidence against usual pharmacological agents is unavailable.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The Grade C supplements statement is neither favorable nor unfavorable and provides no recommended safe dose.

alternative_regimens.name: Vitamin B Complex (B1, B6, B12)
alternative_regimens.summary: Has been evaluated for PDN, but the guideline does not establish an effective or safe recommended dose.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The Grade C supplements statement is neither favorable nor unfavorable; increased vitamin levels can cause neuropathy.

alternative_regimens.name: Benfotiamine
alternative_regimens.summary: Has been evaluated for PDN, but high-level validating studies are lacking.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No separate treatment recommendation is assigned.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The formal supplements statement is graded C, Level II, with Low certainty; it does not endorse or discourage supplementation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients receiving multimodal interdisciplinary care who may benefit from psychological treatment.
decision_rules: Consider psychological approaches as components of interdisciplinary care, not as established stand-alone PDN pain treatments.

recommended_regimens.name: psychological approaches
recommended_regimens.summary: The committee recommends considering psychological treatment within multimodal interdisciplinary care despite limited stand-alone evidence; emotional benefit appears possible.

rows: Acupuncture may be considered in patients with PDN. Some studies including RCTs indicate possible benefit with low adverse event rates.

Lumbar sympathetic block and neurolysis may be considered in patients with PDN. However further studies on safety are needed to validate long term outcomes in treatment patients. Therefore, use of this technique for management of PDN is on a case-by-case basis.

Botulinum toxin injection may be considered as a treatment option for patients with PDN. There are multiple studies that indicate that it may be beneficial in reducing neuropathic pain and improving quality of life. Supplementations (Alpha Lipoic Acid, Acetyl-L-Carnitine, Vitamin B Complex (B1, B6, B12)

Dietary supplements may have a role in helping manage PDN. Further, no recommended dosing is available at this time for safe treatment. Therefore, it is neither advisable or inadvisable at this time.

Intensive glycemic control may delay development or progression of PDN in patients with Type 1 DM but there is little effect on PDN in patients with Type 2 DM. Further, tight glycemic control may result in increased mortality in patients with Type 2 DM. NRS, NPS, Interference Subscale of the WHYMPI (MPI-I), BDI, PSQI, and the Veterans Short Form Survey (SF-36V) were administered pre-treatment and at 12-weeks and 36-weeks postbaseline.

Difference in NRS scores between CBT and control groups at 12 and 36 weeks was not significant. However, NPS pain severity mean change from baseline to 12 weeks was significantly greater in the CBT group compared to the control group, with changes at 36 weeks not reported. Pain interference as measured by the MPII was significantly lower in the CBT group at 36 weeks. Mental health improvement as measured by the SF36V were significantly better than in the control group at 36 weeks, although there were no betweengroup differences at 12 and 36 weeks on the BDI or PSQI.
23 patients received relaxation training (RG), 21 received mindfulness meditation training (MG), 21 were in a control group (CG) that received “attention control education”.

All subjects were administered the VAS, the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue Scale (FACIT-F), and the Neuropathic Pain Impact on Quality of Life Questionnaire (NePIQOL) at baseline, 12 weeks, and 14 weeks.

Pain severity as measured by the VAS was significantly lower in the RG and MG compared to the CG at week 12, and in the RG group at week 14. Fatigue severity as measured by the FACIT-F was significantly worse in the CG compared to the RG at 12 and 14 weeks, although there was no difference in terms of QOL between the MG and CG at both time points.
31 study subjects received mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), 32 were in a control group that received “optimized treatment as usual”, the components of which were unspecified.

All subjects were administered the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ9), the PGIC, the Profile of Mood States-2A (POMS-2A), the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), the PCS, and the NeuroQoL at baseline, 2 weeks postintervention and 3 months post intervention.

MBSR patients were significantly more likely than controls to experience reductions in pain intensity and lower levels of pain interference as measured by the BPI through 12 weeks. They also reported significantly greater impression of improvement through the PGIC. MBSR patients reported significantly greater reductions in catastrophizing (PCS), depression (POMS-2A), and perceived stress (PSS) than controls, and better neuropathyrelated quality of life (NeuroQoL).

All study subjects were females of >55 years of age with PDN. 36 were randomized to the MM group and received 16 session of mindfulness meditation training combined with unspecified “elements of cognitive therapy”. 32 subjects were randomized to the PM group and received 16 sessions of “progressive relaxation meditation”. 37 were randomized to the CM (control meditation) group and received 16 sessions involving discussion and instructions to relax as best as possible.
All subjects completed the Brief Pain Inventory modified for PDN and the PGIC at baseline and 4-week, 8-week, and 12-week follow-ups.

At 12-week follow-up, the MM and PM groups demonstrated significant reductions in pain severity and patient impression of change as measured by the PGIC. MM results were more favorable than those of the PM group. The CM group achieved significant improvement on neither measure.
