artifacts.title: Proposed PDN Treatment Algorithm
artifacts.description: Step 1: Individualize treatment according to comorbidities, diabetes type and severity, and other patient factors; begin with preventive and conservative measures, including glycemic management and early physical therapy such as aerobic or weight-bearing exercise and massage. Step 2: Start oral analgesics after or alongside conservative care; initial options are pregabalin, gabapentin and duloxetine, with careful dose titration and adverse-effect monitoring. Step 3: If meaningful relief is absent or adverse effects are intolerable, consider other oral options while accounting for their risks; opioids are generally not recommended. Step 4: If conservative measures and oral treatments fail, consider topical therapy; the 8% capsaicin patch is described as a reasonable option after failure of at least two proven oral pharmacological agents. Step 5: If pain remains refractory despite conservative, pharmacological and topical treatment, consider interventional options. SCS may be considered when conventional medical management has not helped, with an approximately 7 days temporary trial before permanent implantation; selection of other interventions remains dependent on their more limited evidence.
artifacts.summary: Outlines an individualized progression from glycemic and conservative measures through oral and topical treatments to interventions for refractory PDN.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Clarifies treatment sequencing and the conditions prompting consideration of invasive therapy without presenting limited-evidence options as equivalent to SCS.

document_sections.heading: A Systematic Guideline by the ASPN Workgroup on the Evidence, Education, and Treatment Algorithm for Painful Diabetic Neuropathy: SWEET
document_sections.content: Introduction: Painful diabetic neuropathy (PDN) is a major source of pain and disability worldwide, and its optimal treatment remains unsettled. New pharmacological and interventional options have expanded available care. Objective: SWEET aims to guide clinicians in treating PDN safely and appropriately. Methods: A multidisciplinary international group assembled by the American Society of Pain and Neuroscience (ASPN) searched English-language literature on treatments for diabetic neuropathic pain in Medline, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, BioMed Central, Web of Science, Google Scholar, PubMed, Current Contents Connect, Meeting Abstracts, and Scopus. The search included manuscripts from 2000-present. Results: The group evaluated the evidence and assigned therapy grades to most available PDN treatments using United States Preventive Services Task Force criteria. Conclusion: The guideline reviews available PDN treatments and their safe, appropriate use.

document_sections.heading: Introduction and Methodology Development Process
document_sections.content: ASPN commissioned SWEET to assess evidence, education, and current PDN treatment. Its multidisciplinary group included expertise in Pain Medicine, Neurology, Podiatry, Primary Care, Neurosurgery, Physiatry, Psychology, and Anesthesiology. Topic-specific work groups searched the literature and evaluated peer-reviewed evidence. Authors supplied references and evidence rankings; section leaders assigned recommendation grades, which at least three different SWEET members without conflicts reviewed. Members with identified conflicts had to recuse themselves. ASPN used a modified United States Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF) format for interventional pain treatment. Consensus points were developed through meetings or remote communication. Agreement by at least 80% of contributing authors constituted a quorum; a proposed recommendation with <50% consensus did not achieve consensus. Table 1 defines the modified grading system: A supports providing a service with high certainty of substantial net benefit; B supports providing it when net benefit is moderate with high certainty or moderate to substantial with moderate certainty; C supports selective provision according to professional judgment and patient preferences when at least moderate certainty indicates a small net benefit; D advises against a service when moderate or high certainty indicates no net benefit or harms exceeding benefits; and I Statement indicates insufficient evidence to judge the benefit–harm balance. These recommendations describe best practices, not a standard of care, and require clinical interpretation regardless of evidence strength.

document_sections.heading: Methodology: Literature Search, Evidence Ranking
document_sections.content: The work groups searched worldwide English-language literature in Medline, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, BioMed Central, Web of Science, Google Scholar, PubMed, Current Contents Connect, Meeting Abstracts, and Scopus for studies of diabetic neuropathic pain treatment. They included manuscripts from 2000-present and chose search terms by topic. Peer-reviewed studies received USPSTF quality assessments modified for neuromodulation, followed by a subgroup assessment of certainty about net benefit. Table 2 describes High certainty as consistent findings from well-designed studies in representative primary care populations, with conclusions unlikely to change substantially after future research; its Evidence Level: I-A requires at least one properly designed randomized controlled clinical trial. Moderate certainty permits an assessment of health outcomes but has limitations involving study quantity, size, quality, consistency, generalizability, or coherence; additional evidence might change the estimated effect or conclusion. Its categories are Evidence Level I-B for well-designed controlled nonrandomized clinical trials or prospective observational studies conforming to STROBE criteria, and Evidence Level I-C for retrospective cohorts or large case studies involving >20 subjects. Low certainty means evidence cannot adequately establish effects on health outcomes because of limited or flawed studies, inconsistent findings, gaps, restricted generalizability, or missing important outcomes; Evidence Level II covers expert risk–benefit opinion or case reports. ASPN developed consensus points for major topics. These differ from recommendations based solely on consensus, designated Evidence Level II, which provide expert guidance when stronger study designs are unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Painful Diabetic Neuropathy Background
document_sections.content: PDN is a painful diabetes mellitus (DM) complication involving persistent pain and altered sensation in the extremities. It is reported in as many as 16%–26% of people with diabetes, yet often remains undiscussed and untreated, impairing physical and psychological quality of life. Metabolic and vascular processes contribute to PDN: sustained hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation promote length-dependent nerve injury and pain. Manifestations range from mild discomfort to disabling pain and may include disturbed sleep, anxiety, or depression. Diagnosis draws on symptoms, medical and family history, examination, and additional testing. The history explores symptoms, comorbid conditions, and alternative causes of neuropathic pain; examination assesses sensation, reflexes, and strength. Clinicians may apply Toronto Diabetic Neuropathy Expert Group criteria. Nerve conduction studies evaluate injury and help exclude other neuropathy causes; quantitative sensory testing assesses responses to sensory stimuli and small-fiber function. Laboratory assessment evaluates glycemic control and kidney function and investigates alternatives such as vitamin deficiency or autoimmune disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or nerve ultrasound may identify structural abnormalities or compression. Management is multimodal: tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, opioids, topical 8% capsaicin, lidocaine, or amitriptyline, physical therapy, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, and acupuncture are discussed. Nerve blocks and spinal cord stimulation are emerging options for refractory disease. Despite positions taken by organizations including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Neurology (AAN), opioids remain the most commonly prescribed PDN medication, followed by gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, amitriptyline, and venlafaxine. Treatment should reflect comorbidities and patient preferences and involve relevant primary care, endocrine, interventional pain, podiatric, and other professionals.

document_sections.heading: Physical Exam
document_sections.content: Insidious onset and nonspecific symptoms make early PDN difficult to recognize. Patients commonly describe tingling, electric shocks, numbness, burning, or sensations resembling sandpaper or additional socks beneath the feet. Symptoms often intensify at night and develop in a stocking-glove pattern, starting in the toes and feet before spreading proximally. Early evaluation requires medical and family histories, alcohol and medication histories, and a thorough examination. The American Diabetes Association recommends sensory evaluation with a 128 Hz tuning fork, monofilament, temperature and pinprick testing, deep tendon reflexes, and proprioception. Figure 1 illustrates vibratory testing, the 10g Semmes Weinstein monofilament test, Achilles reflex examination, and foot anatomy, innervation, dermatomes, and sensory territories. Laboratory studies, electrodiagnostic assessment, and skin biopsy may assist diagnosis and monitoring of progression.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Approaches
document_sections.content: The diagnostic approaches discussed encompass sensory, thermal, pinprick, reflex, and proprioceptive assessment, laboratory investigation, electrodiagnostic testing, and skin biopsy.

document_sections.heading: Sensory Testing
document_sections.content: A 128 Hz tuning fork evaluates vibration and large sensory-fiber integrity; absent vibration perception indicates sensory loss. The 10-g Semmes Weinstein monofilament assesses light touch through large fibers and bends under 10 g of pressure. Recommended examination sites include the plantar toes, metatarsal heads, dorsal hallux, midfoot, and plantar heel. Because these examinations assess large fibers, abnormal results usually arise late in disease progression, when changes are irreversible.

document_sections.heading: Thermal Testing
document_sections.content: Temperature-perception testing assesses small fibers affected early in PDN and may help early detection. Reduced temperature sensation has been associated with up to 93% of individuals with glucose intolerance or DM. Subjectivity and lack of standardization limit this approach.

document_sections.heading: Pinprick Sensations
document_sections.content: Pinprick testing probes small myelinated A-delta fibers by checking perception of a sharp stimulus applied with a pin or small-gauge needle. Failure to perceive sharpness indicates abnormal sensation. Although subjective, the test has a high positive predictive value for PDN diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Deep Tendon Reflexes
document_sections.content: Achilles and patellar reflexes have acceptable sensitivity, specificity, and predictive performance in relation to abnormal nerve conduction velocity (NCV). Abnormal responses warrant additional investigation, and available evidence suggests reflex testing can assist early PDN detection.

document_sections.heading: Proprioceptive Testing
document_sections.content: Joint-position testing assesses proprioceptive accuracy in PDN. Studies have linked impaired proprioception with altered diabetic neuropathy scores, supporting its diagnostic usefulness.

document_sections.heading: Laboratory Testing
document_sections.content: At initial presentation or diagnosis, laboratory assessment should include complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic profile, fasting blood glucose, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and vitamin B12. The AAN also suggests serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation because monoclonal gammopathies are associated with peripheral neuropathy. Laboratory findings alone cannot establish PDN, but can screen for alternative causes of peripheral neuropathy.

document_sections.heading: Electrodiagnostic Studies
document_sections.content: After a comprehensive history and examination, nerve conduction velocity testing and electromyography may inform treatment planning. Their value remains debatable when demyelination, nerve entrapment, and nerve injury are not suspected.

document_sections.heading: Skin Biopsies
document_sections.content: A small punch biopsy measuring intraepidermal nerve fiber density is a promising method for diagnosing and monitoring early PDN. Unlike NCV studies, it examines small intraepidermal fibers affected early. The procedure is straightforward and reproducible, and may track progression or indicate treatment response.

document_sections.heading: Section 1. Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: All people with diabetes should be assessed for PDN and treated appropriately if it is present. The principal drug classes are serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), gabapentinoids, and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs). Among oral agents, duloxetine, pregabalin, and tapentadol have FDA approval for PDN. TCAs are used for neuropathic pain, although the section notes a lack of randomized controlled trials specifically for PDN. Opioids may help briefly but are discouraged for chronic noncancer pain. A CDC systematic review found weak to absent support for long-term opioid efficacy in chronic pain, whereas prolonged use was associated with addiction and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Tapentadol has opioid and SNRI-based actions, has demonstrated PDN efficacy, and is FDA-approved, but several societies discourage its use because of long-term opioid risks. SNRIs, gabapentinoids, and TCAs have broadly similar efficacy for neuropathic pain, but individual adverse-effect profiles and indications such as depression or anxiety affect selection. Complete pain elimination is unrealistic, so clinicians should agree on reasonable expectations with patients. Gradual titration may improve tolerance; if no benefit occurs after escalation to the maximum permitted dose for 12 weeks, a drug may be judged ineffective. It should not be dismissed before an adequate dose and trial duration. Evidence for combinations across drug classes is limited. A study compared duloxetine (60 mg/day) plus pregabalin (300 mg/day) with high-dose duloxetine (120 mg/day) and pregabalin (600 mg/day), finding the combination no more effective than individual-agent treatment. Clinicians should weigh potential advantages and disadvantages before combining agents.

document_sections.heading: Individual Pharmacotherapy Agents
document_sections.content: The section examines duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin, TCAs, and tapentadol. Tables 3 and 4 summarize pharmacotherapy studies and ASPN recommendations, including recommendation grades, evidence levels, and certainty about net benefit.

document_sections.heading: Duloxetine
document_sections.content: Duloxetine inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake with balanced activity; these transmitters regulate descending inhibitory pain pathways. It is FDA-approved for PDN and comes in 20 mg, 30 mg, and 60 mg capsules. The FDA target is 60 mg daily; clinical doses range from 20 mg to 120 mg daily. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 24-hour mean pain after 12 weeks improved significantly with duloxetine 60 mg daily or 60 mg twice daily compared with duloxetine 20 mg daily or placebo. A separate randomized open-label study followed patients for 28 weeks and found duloxetine 60 mg twice daily and 120 mg once daily equally effective on the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), with both regimens safe and well tolerated. In another multicenter double-blind study, duloxetine 60 mg daily performed significantly better than pregabalin 300 mg daily across all BPI domains after 8 weeks. Duloxetine is also approved for depression, anxiety, fibromyalgia, and generalized musculoskeletal pain, making it a potentially suitable choice when PDN coexists with these conditions.

document_sections.heading: Gabapentin
document_sections.content: Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant that produces analgesia by binding to and inhibiting the voltage-gated calcium-channel α2δ-1 receptor. Its FDA approvals cover seizures and post-herpetic neuralgia, not PDN, although it is commonly used for PDN. Capsules contain 100 mg, 300 mg, or 400 mg; tablets contain 600 mg or 800 mg; and a liquid preparation contains 250 mg/5 mL for people unable to swallow pills. In one randomized PDN trial, patients received gabapentin 3600 mg daily in three doses or placebo; those unable to tolerate that amount received 900 mg/day, 1200 mg/day, 1800 mg/day, or 2400 mg/day. After 8 weeks, gabapentin improved PDN symptoms relative to placebo on a VAS. Another trial found gabapentin superior to amitriptyline for pain and paresthesia on an NRS; amitriptyline should nevertheless be considered with a concomitant mood disorder because it treats depression. Clinical gabapentin regimens range from 300 mg three times daily to 1200 mg three times daily, with a maximum of 3600 mg/day. Renal elimination requires dose adjustment in renal insufficiency. Because gabapentin may cause peripheral edema, it should not be used in patients who already have peripheral edema.

document_sections.heading: Pregabalin
document_sections.content: Pregabalin is an anticonvulsant with a mechanism similar to gabapentin. It is FDA-approved for neuropathic pain due to PDN, post-herpetic neuralgia, or spinal cord injury, and is also used for fibromyalgia and partial-onset seizures. Available capsules contain 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg, 225 mg, or 300 mg; liquid contains 20 mg/mL. For PDN, the FDA recommends no more than 300 mg per day divided into 3 doses; clinical regimens are individualized while retaining a maximum of 300 mg per day. In a randomized trial, pregabalin 300 mg per day (100 mg three times daily) significantly improved pain VAS scores relative to placebo after 8 weeks.

document_sections.heading: Tricyclic Antidepressants
document_sections.content: TCAs may relieve neuropathic pain through several proposed actions: inhibition of norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake may strengthen inhibitory pain pathways, while blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels may reduce abnormal neuronal firing. A randomized crossover study of 29 patients with PDN and normal or depressed mood compared amitriptyline with placebo over six weeks. From the third to the sixth week, amitriptyline reduced discomfort more than placebo; patients tolerating higher concentrations had greater relief, and 150 mg per day was identified as the optimal daily dose. In a randomized double-blind crossover comparison involving 38 PDN patients, moderate or greater relief at 6 weeks occurred in 74% receiving amitriptyline and 61% receiving desipramine. Its investigators regarded the drugs as equally effective and desipramine as an alternative when amitriptyline was not tolerated. In another randomized double-blind study involving Fifty-one patients, response rates were 73% with amitriptyline and 77% with pregabalin on the McGill and Likert pain scales, without a statistically significant difference. A separate prospective randomized double-blind study of 28 patients compared amitriptyline (25 to 75 mg per day) against gabapentin (900 to 1800 mg per day) for six weeks and found no significant difference in pain relief. TCAs such as amitriptyline may be considered when other recommended treatments are unsuitable, although supporting evidence is limited and one in five patients cannot tolerate treatment. Clinicians should monitor adverse effects, particularly with narrow-angle glaucoma, benign prostatic hypertrophy, orthostasis, urinary retention, impaired hepatic function, or thyroid disease. With additional cardiovascular risk factors, QTc should be assessed because of torsades de pointes risk; prolonged QTc may favor another treatment.

document_sections.heading: Tapentadol
document_sections.content: Tapentadol acts centrally through m-opioid receptor agonism and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and is FDA-approved for PDN. In two randomized controlled trials, patients first underwent a three-week open-label titration. Those achieving ≥1-point reduction in pain intensity on 11 NRS were randomized to tapentadol or placebo. Following a 12-week double-blind maintenance phase, both trials reported effectiveness and safety for moderate-to-severe PDN. Despite FDA approval, the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology clinical Practice Guideline advises against opioids, including tapentadol, for PDN because long-term use carries addiction risk.

document_sections.heading: Section 2. Topical Treatments
document_sections.content: Oral PDN treatments may be limited by substantial adverse effects, a high number-needed-to-treat (NNT), and frequent nonresponse. Topical treatment has therefore gained clinical interest and is often incorporated into care. This section considers lidocaine, capsaicin, and amitriptyline.

document_sections.heading: Topical Lidocaine
document_sections.content: Although the 2021 American Diabetes Association guidelines do not specifically identify topical lidocaine for standard PDN care, it offers a low-risk possibility after FDA-approved treatment fails. As an amide local anesthetic, lidocaine reversibly blocks neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing sodium entry and impulse transmission; its affinity for open and inactive channels preferentially affects hyperexcitable neurons. In an open-label nonrandomized prospective study by Argoff et al involving 41 participants, a 5% lidocaine patch significantly improved pain from baseline over 2 weeks without systemic adverse effects or drug interactions. Barbano et al observed a VAS decrease from 68.6 at baseline to 42.4 at 3 weeks (p < 0.001) in an open-label flexible-dose study with 56 participants. Both studies lacked randomization, blinding, and a control arm. In a randomized open-label multicenter noninferiority comparison of European 5% lidocaine plaster against pregabalin, an interim analysis found similar pain relief. Drug-related adverse events (DRAE) affected 3.9% of the lidocaine arm (n = 47) versus 39.2% of the pregabalin arm (n = 44); discontinuation because of DRAE was reported as 20.3% vs 13.%, respectively. The later full analysis supported the interim findings and reported significantly larger EuroQOL 5-dimension questionnaire (EQ-5D) quality-of-life gains with lidocaine (n = 105) than pregabalin (n = 105). Despite limits to generalizability, topical lidocaine may form part of individualized care when conventional FDA-approved medication fails or adverse effects prevent its use. Table 5 summarizes relevant studies.

document_sections.heading: Topical Capsaicin
document_sections.content: Capsaicin acts on sensory neurons through selective agonism of transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), expressed by nociceptive C and A-delta fibers. At 8% prescription concentration, it activates TRPV1 within the epidermis. Initial depolarization may cause warmth, itching, or pain before nociceptor desensitization. Sustained high-dose exposure increases intracellular calcium and can temporarily impair nociceptor function through membrane-potential loss, receptor desensitization, substance P depletion, and reduced fiber density. Activation of TRPV1 in immune cells may also lessen inflammation. Trials by the Capsaicin Study Group and Tandan et al found 0.075% cream significantly better than placebo over 8 and 12 weeks, respectively; Biesbroeck et al found similar results over 8 weeks. Skin irritation contributed to high dropout in these lower-dose studies. Mou et al reviewed evidence suggesting one application of an 8% patch might relieve focal neuropathic pain for up to 12 weeks. In a randomized trial of 369 patients by Simpson et al, average daily pain changed significantly more from baseline through weeks 2–8 with capsaicin (−27.4%) than placebo (−20.9%) (p<0.001), while adverse-event incidence was similar. In a randomized trial of 50 participants by Anand et al, 8% capsaicin plus standard of care (SOC) significantly improved NRS pain at 3-month follow-up compared with SOC alone. The 8% patch is FDA-approved for PDN and should be considered for moderate relief, especially after initial oral agents fail or help only partly. Table 6 summarizes the trials.

document_sections.heading: Topical Amitriptyline
document_sections.content: Amitriptyline is applied topically for neuropathic pain, including PDN. Its proposed analgesic actions include reduced norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake, antagonism of peripheral and central N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors with reduced glutamate release, and blockade of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels. The topical formulation's precise mechanism is uncertain; skin penetration may produce local and possibly systemic effects. Evidence of efficacy conflicts. In a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled crossover study by Ho et al of 35 people with postsurgical neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, or PDN, topical 5% amitriptyline produced no clinically meaningful pain-score difference from placebo. The total cohort and its PDN subgroup were small. A separate double-blind randomized trial by Kiani et al compared topical 2% amitriptyline with 0.75% capsaicin cream: both improved painful PDN symptoms, but amitriptyline caused fewer DRAE and had better adherence. Topical amitriptyline should not be used first line because efficacy evidence conflicts; it may be warranted after failure of first- and second-line agents given its favorable adverse-effect profile. Tables 7 and 8 present topical-treatment studies and ASPN recommendations; the overall evidence for topical PDN treatments is described as moderate.

document_sections.heading: Section 3. Neuromodulation Spinal Cord Stimulation
document_sections.content: Three studies published in 2014 initially described spinal cord stimulation (SCS) for PDN. In a multicenter randomized trial by de Vos et al, 60 patients with lower-extremity PDN unresponsive to conventional care received medical treatment with or without traditional SCS in a 2:1 allocation. Baseline mean pain VAS was 73 with SCS and 67 in controls; at six months it was 31 with SCS (P<0.001) and remained 67 in controls (P = 0.97). The SCS responder rate was 69%, and EQ-5D and short form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ) findings showed pain, health, and quality-of-life improvements with SCS but not control treatment. In a two-center randomized trial by Slangen et al involving 36 patients with severe lower-limb PDN unresponsive to conventional treatment, 22 received assignment to SCS plus medical therapy and 14 to best medical therapy (BMT). Implantation required a successful stimulation trial, achieved by 77% of SCS patients. At six months, success meant ≥50% daytime or nighttime relief or a rating of “(very) much improved” for pain and sleep on the patient global impression of change (PGIC). Success occurred in 59% with SCS versus 7% with BMT (P < 0.01). Daytime and nighttime pain relief occurred in 41 and 36% with SCS versus 0 and 7% with BMT, respectively (P < 0.05). Pain and sleep were rated “(very) much improved” by 55 and 36% with SCS, respectively, with no corresponding BMT improvement (P < 0.001 and P < 0.05). Another 2014 study by de Vos et al switched patients treated with traditional SCS for six months to burst SCS for two weeks. Of 48 participants, 12 had PDN: their baseline VAS was 70, compared with 28 during traditional SCS (P<0.001) and 16 during burst SCS (P<0.001); the difference between stimulation modes was significant (P<0.05). Burst effects were greater for PDN than failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS), 77% vs 57%, and eight of the 12 PDN patients had more relief with burst than traditional SCS. No other PDN burst-SCS studies had been published at the time described. A prospective multicenter study by Van Beek et al followed 48 patients for five years. Treatment success, defined by 50% NRS reduction or significant PGIC improvement, occurred in 55% at five years; 80% of permanent-implant recipients still used SCS then. Higher Michigan Diabetic Neuropathy Score (MDNS) was associated with failure during follow-up (P = 0.014). In the multicenter open-label randomized SENZA-PDN study by Petersen et al, 216 patients were allocated 1:1 to 10 kHz high frequency (HF)-SCS plus conventional medical management (CMM) or CMM alone; 113 entered the treatment arm and 103 the control arm. At six months, >50% relief without neurological deterioration occurred in 78.9% (75/95) of HF-SCS patients and 5.3% (5/94) of CMM patients (P < 0.001). Following permitted crossover at six months, the 12-month implanted-patient analysis reported average relief of 74.3% and >50% relief without further neurological decline in 85%; quality-of-life, sleep, pain-interference, and functioning measures improved at six and 12 months. At 24 months, investigators reported a mean pain reduction of 79.9% from baseline and >50% relief in 90.1%, alongside better quality of life, sleep, and neurological symptoms; 3.2% of implants were removed because of infection. A systematic review of nineteen studies and 376 SCS implant recipients with length-dependent peripheral neuropathies, including conditions beyond PDN, reported significant pain-intensity improvement from baseline after 12 months in every included study. Its Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) assessment rated this wider-neuropathy outcome very low quality, underscoring the need for better trials. Traditional SCS and HF-SCS have each outperformed conventional medical management for PDN pain in randomized trials. Tables 9 and 10 summarize the evidence and ASPN recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Peripheral Nerve Stimulation
document_sections.content: Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) is considered a possible PDN alternative to drug therapy. Published PDN-specific evidence remains limited, and further study is needed.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: PNS has been described for neuropathic pain, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), phantom and residual-limb pain, low back pain, and postoperative pain. It may not suit diffuse PDN spanning several nerve territories or a large dermatomal area because current systems accommodate only 1 or 2 leads. Larger mixed nerves such as the sciatic nerve can sometimes be targeted, but stimulating afferent Aβ fibers without recruiting efferent Aα motor fibers may be difficult. PNS may benefit patients who cannot undergo SCS or dorsal root ganglion stimulation (DRG-S) because of complex spinal anatomy, previous spinal surgery or fusion, or inability to stop anticoagulants. Depending on lead location and adjacent vessels or critical structures, it is considered low to intermediate risk; in many cases it can be performed without stopping blood-thinning medication. Temporary and permanent systems are available.

document_sections.heading: Nerve Targets and Patient Considerations
document_sections.content: Relatively focal PDN pain may make a patient suitable for PNS. Predominantly plantar-foot pain, for example, may be addressed through the tibial nerve. That nerve passes from the popliteal fossa through the deep posterior leg compartment and tarsal tunnel, then divides into the lateral plantar nerve (LPN), medial plantar nerve (MPN), and medial calcaneal nerve (MCN). Leads are generally placed behind the tibia and proximal to the tarsal tunnel. Other possible lower-extremity targets are the common peroneal, superficial peroneal, and sciatic nerves; median and ulnar nerves are possible upper-extremity targets. SCS and DRG-S studies have mainly addressed lower-extremity PDN. The tibial and common peroneal nerves may be entrapped at the tarsal tunnel and fibular head, respectively. Increased compression in diabetes has been proposed to contribute to injury and irreversible sensory change. Decompression neurolysis of upper- and lower-extremity nerves in people with diabetes has yielded promising results. PNS may be an option when focal pain persists after decompression; placing leads proximal to a suspected lesion, entrapment, or injury is advisable.

document_sections.heading: Current Evidence for PNS in PDN
document_sections.content: PDN-specific PNS evidence is still developing, and treatment protocols and stimulation parameters need standardization. A recent review identified grade II-3 evidence from three retrospective or prospective cohorts supporting tibial-nerve PNS in the lower leg. An older study of percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (PENS) targeting the tibial and deep peroneal nerves reported pain improvement. Larger, well-designed trials with longer follow-up are needed to determine durability and adverse effects.

document_sections.heading: Future Directions
document_sections.content: PNS appears promising for PDN, particularly when localized pain corresponds to a single nerve, but standardized protocols, long-term effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness require further investigation. Table 11 summarizes PNS studies in PDN, including pain outcomes and evidence levels.

document_sections.heading: #### Peripheral Nerve Stimulation
document_sections.content: Table 12 presents the ASPN recommendation for PNS in PDN. The evidence is developing but suggests that PNS could help patients whose pain is localized to the territory of a single nerve. Standardized treatment protocols, longer-term efficacy and safety data, and cost-effectiveness assessments are still needed. The SWEET Consensus Committee recommends considering PNS for focal lower-extremity PDN after conservative therapies have failed when the patient is not a candidate for SCS (Grade C; level of evidence 1-C; Moderate certainty of net benefit).

document_sections.heading: #### DRG Stimulation
document_sections.content: DRG-S is approved for CRPS and/or peripheral causalgia affecting the groin and lower limb; its use for PDN is still developing. The proposed analgesic actions include modulation of Aδ and C fibers and Aβ collaterals, use of sensory convergence in the dorsal horn, normalization of abnormal DRG neuronal sensitivity, and suppression of inflammatory responses, particularly those mediated by glial cells. Experimental animal studies have examined DRG stimulation for PDN. Compared with SCS, DRG-S may cover a focal painful area with less stimulation outside it by recruiting sensory neurons serving the affected distal region. Evidence across causes of PN comprises a small prospective study, three retrospective case series, five case reports, and two further case series involving patients with multiple pain causes. Within that literature, two retrospective studies and one case report specifically address PDN. In the retrospective report by Eldabe et al, seven patients with PDN received implants; two underwent explantation at or before the one-week visit because of inadequate coverage or personal reasons. Among the seven implanted patients, three had ≥50% pain reduction at six months, including two with more than 80% reduction. At 12 months, two had ≥50% reduction and one was lost to follow-up. Falowski et al retrospectively assessed eight patients with intractable leg and/or foot PN who had responded to an L4-S1 DRG-S trial. Two had PDN, but outcomes were not reported separately for them. Across all eight patients, two reported 100% relief, two better than 80%, another three better than 50%, and one better than 40%. Chapman et al described one patient with PDN and low back pain whose 7-day unilateral T12 and S1 trial reduced foot-pain VAS from 9 to 0 and significantly improved ODI, EQ-5D, and SF-36; implantation outcomes were unavailable. Retrospective designs, absence of blinding, and small samples limit the PDN evidence. The guideline calls for more research and advises selective, judicious use according to professional judgment and previously unsuccessful treatment. Tables 13 and 14 summarize the studies and recommendation. DRG-S may be considered for lower-extremity PDN after other FDA approved treatments fail (Grade C; level of evidence II; Low certainty of net benefit).

document_sections.heading: #### Intrathecal Drug Delivery
document_sections.content: Ziconotide is a nonopioid analgesic that binds N-type voltage-sensitive calcium channels and reversibly prevents nociceptive afferents from releasing glutamate, CGRP, and substance P in the spinal dorsal horn. Its clinically available administration route is intrathecal. It does not act on mu-opioid receptors, so naloxone does not reverse its effects; long-term use has shown no tolerance, and abrupt cessation does not produce withdrawal. FDA labeling permits administration by a microambulatory delivery device. PACC recommends an initial 0.5–1.2 mcg/day, while product labeling permits an initial dose as high as 2.4 mcg/day. Because the therapeutic window is narrow, the recommended increase is 0.5–1.0 mcg/day every several days, up to 21.6 μg/day. A black box warning contraindicates ziconotide in patients with a history of psychosis, making psychiatric evaluation necessary before a trial. Adverse effects, more frequent at higher doses, include nausea, vomiting, confusion, postural hypotension, gait abnormality, urinary retention, nystagmus, drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, visual changes, and increased serum creatine kinase. Three randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled studies support intrathecal ziconotide for non-cancer-related pain; approximately 75% of participants had neuropathic pain. A prospective 2021 study of 14 patients reported improvements in pain, emotional aspects, disability, emotional well-being, and catastrophizing. Table 15 summarizes the intrathecal literature, and Table 16 presents the recommendation. The SWEET guidelines support careful patient selection for intrathecal ziconotide in diabetic neuropathic pain while noting that no published study specifically tests its effectiveness for PDN. The stated support for intrathecal ziconotide in diabetic neuropathy is limited (Grade C; level of evidence I-C; Low certainty of net benefit).

document_sections.heading: #### Sub-Topic: Special Considerations for Implantable Therapies in the Diabetic Patient
document_sections.content: DM increases perioperative morbidity and mortality. Surgical stress can alter glucose metabolism and cause acute hyperglycemia in up to 40% of patients undergoing noncardiac surgery. Poorly controlled DM impairs soft-tissue and tendon healing and raises concern for wound complications and surgical-site infection. Chronic hyperglycemia is linked to reduced neutrophil phagocytosis, greater inflammation and oxidative stress, impaired endothelial function, and relative immune compromise. Reduced innate immunity is identified as a key contributor to infection around implanted devices. Surgical technique also matters for preventing infection, seroma, and wound dehiscence, complications for which patients with diabetes have increased risk. Evidence from orthopedic and cardiac surgery informs discussion of implant outcomes in pain medicine and neurosurgery. Reported surgical-site infection incidence among chronic-pain implantable devices ranges from 1% to 17%; patients with diabetes have increased risk of severe infection. SCS infection rates have been reported as high as 3.11% within 12 months. Hoelzer et al found an overall SCS implant infection rate of 2.45%, including patients with diabetes, without separating controlled from uncontrolled DM. Implant-associated biofilm and the initial innate immune response contribute to infection. Potential impairments include absent vascularization at the device interface, surgery-related disruption of nearby blood flow, local hypoxia, abnormal phagocyte function on foreign material, inadequate signaling between biomaterial and host cells, and microbial attachment that protects organisms from phagocytosis; DM affects these factors. A1C can help identify poorly controlled DM, but no A1C threshold for elective surgery has clear consensus. The relative importance of longstanding versus acute perioperative hyperglycemia remains debated. Underwood et al associated A1C >8% with worse surgical outcomes, and Gabriel et al associated that threshold with more postoperative surgical-site infections. Severe, prolonged perioperative hyperglycemia may cause more operative complications than acute hyperglycemia alone. Tables 17 and 18 summarize the supporting literature and ASPN recommendations. Those recommendations call for preoperative A1c measurement in patients with diabetes undergoing elective surgery and postponement when A1C is above 8; each has Grade B, level of evidence I-C, and Moderate certainty of net benefit.

document_sections.heading: #### Non-Invasive Neuromodulation
document_sections.content: Historical reports described stimulation of living tissue by a changing magnetic field in 1896, magnetic nerve stimulation in 1973, and mPNS in 1982. Compared with ePNS, mPNS was described as painless and capable of reaching deeper nerves. Magnetic stimulation does not produce the skin-surface hydrolysis and pH changes associated with potentially damaging high current densities during electrical stimulation. Its changing 3D magnetic field produces a larger electrical field than the more 2D field of ePNS and, at stimulation threshold, recruits more Aβ fibers without recruiting Aδ fibers. An initial mPNS pilot included 24 patients with neuropathic pain, including PDN. The treatment wand was held on or immediately above the skin. Treatment comprised three consecutive daily sessions during the first week, then weekly sessions to complete 6 treatments in the first month, sessions every second week in the second month, and monthly sessions when pain flared. Two-thirds met the responder definition of 50% or more VAS pain reduction; responders experienced 87% pain-score reduction. Mean VAS reduction from baseline was 3.8, and 58.3% of responders reduced opioid use. A randomized prospective study available as a 2023 ASPN meeting abstract reported 90-day data. Its PDN subgroup included 13 patients receiving mPNS plus CMM and 4 receiving CMM alone. Response meant >50% pain relief at 3 months. On a per-protocol basis, 8 out of 8 treated patients responded, with a 64.7% decrease in their pain scores. In the control arm, 1 out of 4 responded and mean pain scores increased by 2.4%. The guideline regards mPNS as a promising painless, noninvasive option but notes that a randomized sham-controlled prospective study in lower-extremity diabetic PN is ongoing. Tables 19 and 20 summarize the evidence and recommendation: mPNS may provide intermediate-term (3 months) relief for PDN-related neuropathic pain (Grade B; level of evidence I-B; Moderate certainty of net benefit).

document_sections.heading: ### Section 4. Alternative Approaches
document_sections.content: Nonimplantable interventions, supplements, and lifestyle changes considered for PDN include acupuncture, sympathetic nerve procedures, and botulinum toxin injections. Moderate-level evidence favors acupuncture as an optional approach, with prospective studies and RCTs suggesting benefit and relatively few adverse events. One single-blinded placebo-controlled RCT found a low-to-moderate effect against sham without appreciable adverse effects. Another RCT found pain improvement at week 12 versus standard care, with waning efficacy by week 18. Studies of electroacupuncture reported less pain and better sleep and quality of life; laser acupuncture improved nerve conduction and patient-reported outcomes against placebo. Reports of Saussureae Involucratae Herba injections at acupuncture points and perineural platelet rich plasma also describe symptom improvement but require validation. Meta-analyses support acupuncture findings while calling for longer-term efficacy studies. If acupuncture is tried, the semi-standardized ACUDPN protocol using bilateral points is recommended. Evidence for lumbar sympathetic block or neurolysis is sparse. A case report described improved bilateral leg PDN after nine continuous blocks over 26 months. An RCT suggested better pain outcomes with continuous lumbar sympathetic block followed by alcohol neurolysis than with alcohol neurolysis alone, persisting at 6 months. Another comparison reported complete remission rates of 66.7%, 73.3%, and 93.3% with alcohol neurolysis, radiofrequency thermocoagulation, and their combination, respectively, without severe complications; pain returned at 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year, respectively. Its authors considered the combined approach safe and effective. These procedures may be options for selected refractory cases before more invasive care. Limited studies of botulinum toxin injections suggest benefit without major complications. Botulinum toxin type A blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions and may alter sensory signaling through reduced glutamate, CGRP, and substance P release. An RCT found less neuropathic foot pain and better quality of life and sleep after intradermal injection than with control treatment. Other studies reported tolerability and significant pain reduction versus saline. A meta-analysis described level I evidence for a small improvement, particularly on the foot dorsum; because the effect is small, botulinum toxin A should be considered only as an adjunct to first-line approaches. Injection for PDN is not FDA approved. Most supplements discussed are antioxidants or neuroprotective cofactors. Studies of Alpha-lipoic acid report improvement with long-term treatment, but efficacy has not been compared with usual PDN drugs. Acetyl-L-carnitine has been used successfully for PDN and other neuropathic pain, but high-grade comparative evidence is unavailable. Vitamin B complex (B1, B6, B12) has been investigated for antioxidant and neural effects; no safe recommended dose is established, and elevated levels can themselves cause neuropathy. High-level validation is also lacking for Benfotiamine. Lifestyle management emphasizes glycemic control. Intensive control can delay PDN development or progression in T1DM but has little effect on PDN in T2DM. DCCT reported a −1.84 annualized risk difference with tight control in T1DM; ACCORD and VADT reported a −0.058 annualized risk difference for T2DM that was not statistically significant. Hemoglobin A1C below 6.0 has been associated with increased mortality, whereas a range between 7.0 and 8.0 has been recommended. Weight loss and exercise have increased intraepidermal nerve fiber density, which is ordinarily reduced in PDN; improved diet and an active lifestyle are advocated to lessen symptom severity. Tables 21 and 22 summarize the cited studies and ASPN recommendations for alternative approaches.

document_sections.heading: #### Psychological/Behavioral
document_sections.content: PDN has physical, social, and psychological consequences, making multidisciplinary care likely more effective than a single treatment. Depression, anxiety, catastrophization, and poorer QOL have been documented alongside PDN; these factors may mediate pain experience. Addressing psychological consequences could improve emotional comfort, but this review concentrates on whether psychological treatment reduces pain severity, the experience of pain, or pain interference. Approaches studied include CBT, MT in the forms of MM or MBSR, and ACT.

document_sections.heading: #### RCTs
document_sections.content: Teixeira’s 2010 pilot RCT of MM found significant QOL improvement against control but no significant relative change in pain severity or unpleasantness; the author identified numerous methodological limitations. In the initial CBT RCT, published by Otis et al in 2013, the CBT group improved significantly from pretreatment to 4-month follow-up in pain severity and interference, unlike usual-care controls. Neither group showed a significant change in depressive symptoms. The pilot included only 12 treated and 8 control participants, and the small, insignificant pain differences do not provide strong evidence. A 2020 Iranian RCT of ACT found significantly better pain perception and acceptance than control immediately after treatment and at 3 months. Its authors cautioned that exclusions and substantial dropout left a small sample and could have biased selection; it was the only identified RCT addressing ACT and pain perception. Table 23 summarizes published RCTs of psychological treatments for PDN pain outcomes. Table 24 presents the group recommendation: psychological approaches may be considered despite sparse evidence as stand-alone PDN treatment; possible emotional benefits and an extremely low risk:benefit ratio support providing them within multimodal interdisciplinary care (Grade C; level of evidence I1-B; Moderate certainty of net benefit).

document_sections.heading: #### Systematic Reviews
document_sections.content: Few informative systematic reviews are available because meaningful RCTs on psychological treatment of PDN pain are scarce. A 2015 Cochrane review of psychological care for chronic neuropathic pain included only 2 studies, neither involving PDN. A 2016 Italian neurorehabilitation consensus review considered just one study and stated that CBT may be used for diabetic neuropathy and neuropathic pain associated with cancer or HIV; it assigned D evidence, described as evidence level 3 or 4 or extrapolation from studies rated 2+, alongside GPP based on the development group’s clinical experience. A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis of CBT and MT found significantly less pain in intervention than control groups immediately after treatment, but no significant between-group difference at follow-up ≥2 weeks. It found no immediate between-group difference in pain interference, although the CBT/MT groups had significantly less interference at 24-week follow-up. The guideline judges that review methodologically seriously flawed, including questionable selection of studies.

document_sections.heading: ### Section 5. Algorithmic Approach
document_sections.content: The proposed PDN algorithm requires individualization for comorbidities, diabetes type and severity, and other patient factors. Its first tier combines prevention and conservative care. PDN follows a variable course, but persistent hyperglycemia may drive nerve dysfunction and painful hyperexcitability; addressing it is therefore a reasonable first step. Glycemic control may prevent PDN and may partly reverse or modify symptoms after they develop. High-quality evidence in type 1 diabetes associates intensive control with lower odds of distal symmetric polyneuropathy than conventional insulin therapy. For type 2 diabetes, intensive control has not consistently prevented or treated PDN symptoms and may increase hypoglycemia risk. Physical therapy, including sustained aerobic and weight-bearing exercise and massage, should be offered early because it may improve motor and sensory neuropathy, balance, and quality of life. Oral analgesics are commonly started afterward or alongside conservative measures. First-line options are the gabapentinoids pregabalin and gabapentin and the SNRI duloxetine; careful dose escalation and surveillance for dizziness, sedation, and other adverse effects are warranted. If relief is inadequate or adverse effects intolerable, second- or third-line oral drugs may be tried. FDA-approved tapentadol carries opioid risks. TCAs such as amitriptyline and nortriptyline may relieve pain but commonly cause neurological and cardiac adverse effects. Opioids are generally not recommended because short-term analgesia is modest and risks include respiratory depression, sedation, opioid use disorder, and constipation. Topical treatment can be considered when conservative and oral options fail. The 8% capsaicin patch is FDA approved for PDN of the feet; application-site reactions may affect over 30% of patients, although tolerability measures are available. Given its noninvasive nature and safety profile, 8% topical capsaicin is presented as a reasonable first-line option after at least two proven oral drugs fail. Persistent pain despite conservative care, topical therapy, and pharmacologic treatment, such as a trial of at least 1–2 analgesics, warrants consideration of intervention. Neuromodulation may disrupt symptom signaling at peripheral nerves, the dorsal root ganglion, or spinal dorsal columns. Modalities discussed include t-SCS, 10-kHz SCS, and stimulation targeted to the brain, dorsal root ganglion, or peripheral nerves.

document_sections.heading: ## Proposed PDN Treatment Algorithm
document_sections.content: Figure 2 depicts the proposed management algorithm. t-SCS, also called tonic SCS, uses a low-frequency cycle above the perception threshold; PDN data suggest modest-to-moderate efficacy. Subthreshold approaches are not consciously perceived and include 10-kHz SCS and burst-SCS. Level 1 evidence supports significant benefit from 10-kHz SCS versus CMM alone, including improvements in secondary outcomes and health-related quality of life through 12 months. Burst-SCS with passive recharge uses high-frequency spike trains in cycles intended to resemble thalamic Theta bursts. In a crossover comparison, De Vos found burst-SCS more effective than t-SCS in a subset switched after at least six months of continuous t-SCS, but PDN-specific study remains limited. DRG-S evidence is likewise limited: Eldabe et al reported on 10 patients and described VAS declines of 48 at one month and 49 at six months, with substantial participant attrition. NIS or mPNS has been investigated for PDN symptoms and function, but evidence for exogenous stimulation or magnetism remains limited; ongoing studies may clarify whether its noninvasive nature and favorable safety profile justify earlier use. IDD is established for chronic intractable pain, for which ziconotide and morphine are the only FDA-approved drugs identified here. This algorithmic discussion states that evidence supporting IDD specifically for PDN does not exist, while guidelines support its use for chronic intractable axial-spine and leg pain. Overall, SCS is described as superior to CMM alone for PDN. Evidence indicates modest-to-substantial efficacy for 10-kHz SCS and t-SCS, which may be considered after CMM fails. A temporary trial of approximately 7 days before permanent surgical implantation offers a way to assess likely benefit.

document_sections.heading: ### Conclusion
document_sections.content: The ASPN SWEET Guideline brings pharmacological, interventional, and alternative PDN approaches together in a comprehensive clinical tool. It aims to improve appropriate and safe care for a difficult, undertreated condition. The guideline states that recent drug and interventional developments have improved the ability to relieve PDN pain and suffering, while further research is needed to identify optimal treatment. ASPN intends broad clinician access and dissemination through its website and other channels. The guideline is intended to remain current, with updates at least every 12 months and when important new evidence appears.
